Patient demographics:
  age: 38
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Middle Eastern
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Hairdresser
  trauma_type: Life-threatening illness
  pcl5: 37

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Visual (Photos): Related photos, Dream Residue: Waking up from a nightmare, Medical Procedures: Undergoing a medical examination or procedure
  Threat: Negative Emotions: Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame, Body on Alert: My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger, Physical Reactivity: Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience
  Memory: Olfactory Recall: When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened., Pain Recall: When the memory returns I feel physical pain in the same parts of my body as during the event, Emotion Without Image: Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory
  Negative Appraisals: Body as Enemy: My body keeps reacting as if I am still in danger even when I am safe, Fear Going Crazy: My reactions since the event mean that I am going crazy, Body Unreliable: I can no longer trust my own body

Vignette:
Ali, a 38-year-old Middle Eastern man and single hairdresser, has been struggling with the aftermath of a life-threatening illness that occurred several years ago. The experience left him with a profound sense of vulnerability and anxiety that has persisted ever since. The traumatic event began when Ali was admitted to the hospital for severe complications from an autoimmune disease. He spent weeks in a sterile environment, surrounded by medical equipment, and subjected to constant monitoring and procedures. The hospital smelled of antiseptic and medicinal odors, which were overpowering and often triggered his memories of that time. Upon waking up from a nightmare about his illness, Ali would find himself drenched in sweat, heart pounding as if he was still fighting for survival. His body felt constantly tense and ready to react to any perceived danger, even though the threat had long passed. The memory of the sterile hospital environment often resurfaced, and with it came the sharp smell of antiseptics that seemed to linger in his mind like a ghostly presence. In the weeks following his discharge, Ali found himself avoiding anything that reminded him of his time in the hospital. He refused to undergo routine medical examinations or procedures, even though he knew they were necessary for his ongoing health. This avoidance was not just about fear but also about the intense physical reactions it would trigger—his heart would race, and he would feel dizzy and nauseous. At work, Ali's constant state of hyperarousal made it difficult to focus on his clients. The sight of a blood sample or even the sound of a medical alert could send him into a panic. He had come to believe that his body was still reacting as if he were in danger, which only reinforced his fear that something was fundamentally wrong with him. The emotional toll was equally devastating. When Ali thought about the frightening event, he often felt physical pain in the same parts of his body where he experienced discomfort during his illness. Sometimes, he would feel the full intensity of the emotions—fear, horror, and shame—without any clear image or memory to anchor them. This made him believe that he was losing control, going crazy. His relationships suffered as well. He had become more withdrawn and irritable at work, which strained his interactions with colleagues and clients. Ali's fear of being seen as unstable or untrustworthy led him to avoid social gatherings, further isolating himself from others. What finally brought Ali to seek help was a particularly distressing episode where he had a panic attack during a routine appointment for a check-up. The combination of the medical setting, the smell of antiseptics, and his body's automatic response overwhelmed him. He realized that his fear was not only affecting his daily life but also preventing him from living normally. Ali is most afraid of losing control completely and becoming unable to function as a hairdresser or in any other aspect of his life. However, he is also hopeful that with help, he can regain some sense of normalcy and trust in himself again. He hopes to find ways to manage the intense emotions and physical reactions without avoiding everything that reminds him of his illness. Ali’s journey is marked by a deep-seated fear that his body will betray him at any moment, making it difficult for him to trust his own senses and abilities. His hope lies in learning how to navigate these fears and regain control over his life.
